## 5.1. Load and inspect the iris dataset

```{r}
data("iris")
head(iris)
str(iris)
names(iris)
```

## 5.2. Measures of central tendency

### 5.2.1 and 5.2.2 Mean and median by species

```{r}
library(dplyr)

iris %>% group_by(Species) %>% summarise( Mean = mean(Sepal.Length),
Median = median(Sepal.Length) )
```

### 5.2.3 Mode function

```{r}
mode_function <- function(x) { frequencies <- table(x)
names(frequencies)[which.max(frequencies)] }
```

# 5.2.3 Mode by species

```{r}
iris %>% group_by(Species) %>% summarise(Mode =
mode_function(Sepal.Length))
```

### Guide Questions

1.  Setosa has the lowest mean sepal length at 5.01 cm, while virginica
    has the highest at 6.59 cm.
2.  For setosa, the mean is 5.01 cm and the median is 5.0 cm. For
    versicolor, the mean is 5.94 cm and the median is 5.9 cm. For
    virginica, the mean is 6.59 cm and the median is 6.5 cm. The mean
    and median are close for all three species.
3.  The median is less affected by extreme values because it represents
    the middle value of the data. The mean can be pulled higher or lower
    by unusually large or small observations.
4.  The mode is the value that occurs most frequently, while the mean is
    the average and the median is the middle value when the data are
    arranged in order.

## 5.3 Measures of variability

### Range, Variance, SD, and IQR

```{r}
iris %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  summarise(
    Minimum = min(Sepal.Length),
    Maximum = max(Sepal.Length),
    Range = max(Sepal.Length) - min(Sepal.Length),
    Variance = var(Sepal.Length),
    SD = sd(Sepal.Length),
    Q1 = quantile(Sepal.Length, 0.25),
    Q3 = quantile(Sepal.Length, 0.75),
    IQR = IQR(Sepal.Length)
  )
```

### Guide Questions

5.  Virginica has the largest range at 3.0 cm, followed by versicolor at
    2.1 cm and setosa at 1.5 cm.
6.  Virginica has the largest standard deviation at approximately
    0.64 cm. This indicates that its sepal lengths are more spread out
    from the mean compared to the other species.
7.  The range measures the difference between the maximum and minimum
    values, while the IQR measures the spread of the middle 50% of the
    data.
8.  The median and IQR are less affected by extreme values than the mean
    and standard deviation. Using them together gives a more reliable
    description of the center and spread of skewed data.

## 5.4 Frequency distribution

### 5.4.1 Freq Table

```{r}
species_freq <- table(iris$Species)
species_freq
```

### 5.4.2 Relative frequency and percentage

```{r}
prop.table(species_freq)
prop.table(species_freq) * 100
```

### 5.4.3 Counts and percentages in a single table

```{r}
iris %>%
  count(Species, name = "Frequency") %>%
  mutate(Percentage = round(Frequency / sum(Frequency) * 100, 2))
```

### Guide Questions

9.  Each species has 50 flowers, giving a total of 150 flowers in the
    dataset.
10. Setosa, versicolor, and virginica each represent 33.33% of the
    dataset.
11. Percentages allow researchers to compare the relative proportions of
    groups even when the datasets have different sample sizes.

## 5.5 Measures of distribution

```{r}
library(e1071)

### 5.5.1 Calculate skewness and kurtosis
iris %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  summarise(
    Skewness = skewness(Sepal.Length),
    Kurtosis = kurtosis(Sepal.Length)
  )
```

### Guide Questions

12. Setosa has the most positive skewness at approximately 0.113, while
    versicolor has the most negative skewness at approximately 0.099.
    However, all three skewness values are positive, so none is actually
    negatively skewed. Versicolor simply has the smallest positive
    skewness value.
13. Positive skewness indicates a longer tail toward the right, while
    negative skewness indicates a longer tail toward the left. A
    skewness value near zero generally indicates a more symmetrical
    distribution.
14. Kurtosis describes the shape of a distribution, particularly its
    tails and how it compares with a normal distribution.
15. Skewness and kurtosis summarize certain features of a distribution,
    but they do not show its full shape. Histograms and boxplots help
    identify patterns, multiple peaks, and possible outliers that these
    numerical values may not reveal.

## 5.6 Visualizing the data

### 5.6.1 Histogram

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ Species) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Sepal Length by Iris Species",
    x = "Sepal Length (cm)",
    y = "Frequency"
  )
```

### Guide Questions

16. Setosa has the lowest sepal lengths and the smallest spread.
    Versicolor has intermediate sepal lengths, while virginica has the
    highest sepal lengths and the greatest overall range.
17. Setosa appears relatively concentrated and approximately
    symmetrical. Versicolor and virginica show more variation and some
    overlap in their sepal lengths. Their exact shapes, including any
    skewness or multiple peaks, should be confirmed using the
    histograms.

### 5.6.2 Boxplots

```{r}
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Sepal Length by Iris Species",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Sepal Length (cm)"
  )
```

### Guide Questions

18. Virginica has the largest IQR at approximately 0.675 cm, indicating
    the greatest variability in the middle 50% of its sepal length
    observations.
19. Yes, a potential outlier is visible in virginica, shown as a point
    below the lower whisker of the boxplot. No potential outliers are
    visible for setosa or versicolor.
20. The boxplot makes it easier to compare the median, spread, and
    potential outliers among species. The histogram provides more detail
    about the distribution's shape and frequency.

## 5.7 Practice Exercise: Summarizing data using the CO2 dataset

### Load packages and dataset

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(e1071)
```

### 5.7.1 Inspect the dataset

```{r}
?CO2
data(CO2)
data("CO2", package = "datasets")
head(CO2)
dim(CO2)
```

How many observations and variables are in the dataset?

- The CO₂ dataset has 84 observations and 5 variables.

Which variables are numerical, and which are categorical?

- The numerical variables are conc and uptake, while Plant, Type, and Treatment are categorical variables.

What does the variable uptake measure?

- The uptake variable measures the rate of carbon dioxide uptake by the plants, expressed in µmol m⁻² s⁻¹.

### 5.7.2 Mean and median

```{r}
CO2 %>%
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(uptake),
    Median = median(uptake)
  )

CO2 %>%
  group_by(Treatment) %>%
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(uptake),
    Median = median(uptake)
  )
```

How do the mean and median compare for the entire dataset?

- The overall mean uptake is 27.21, while the median is 28.3. The mean is slightly lower than the median.

How do mean uptake values compare between the two treatment groups?

- The nonchilled treatment has a higher mean uptake of 30.6 compared to 23.8 for the chilled treatment. This suggests that the plants in the nonchilled treatment generally had higher CO₂ uptake.

Why should these summaries be interpreted descriptively rather than as proof that the treatments differ statistically?

- These summaries only describe the observed data. They do not establish whether the difference between treatments is statistically significant, which would require further statistical analysis.

### 5.7.3 Variability by treatment

```{r}
CO2 %>%
  group_by(Treatment) %>%
  summarise(
    Minimum = min(uptake),
    Maximum = max(uptake),
    Range = max(uptake) - min(uptake),
    Variance = var(uptake),
    SD = sd(uptake),
    IQR = IQR(uptake)
  )
```

Which treatment group has the larger range?

- The nonchilled treatment has a slightly larger range of 34.9, compared
  to 34.7 for the chilled treatment.

Which group has the larger standard deviation?

- The chilled treatment has the larger standard deviation of 10.9,
  compared to 9.70 for the nonchilled treatment. This indicates that the
  uptake values in the chilled group are more spread out around their
  mean.

How do the SD and IQR provide different information about variability?

- The standard deviation measures how spread out the observations are
  around the mean, while the IQR measures the spread of the middle 50%
  of the data. The IQR is less affected by extreme values.

### 5.7.4 Frequency and percentage

```{r}
CO2 %>%
  count(Treatment, name = "Frequency") %>%
  mutate(Percentage = round(Frequency / sum(Frequency) * 100, 2))
``` 

### 5.7.5 Skewness and kurtosis
```{r}
CO2 %>%
  summarise(
    Skewness = skewness(uptake),
    Kurtosis = kurtosis(uptake)
  )
```

How many observations belong to each treatment group, and what
percentage of the dataset does each group represent?

- Both the chilled and nonchilled treatments have 42 observations each,
  representing 50% of the dataset.

Does the frequency table describe the distribution of uptake values or
the number of observations in each treatment? Explain.

- The frequency table describes the number of observations in each
  treatment, not the distribution of uptake values. It shows how many
  observations belong to each group and their percentages.

What are the skewness and kurtosis values for the overall uptake
distribution? What does the sign of the skewness suggest about the
distribution?

- The skewness is approximately -0.104, while the kurtosis is
  approximately -1.348. The negative skewness indicates that the
  distribution is nearly symmetrical, with a slight tail toward the
  lower uptake values.

Why should these numerical measures be interpreted alongside a
histogram?

- Skewness and kurtosis summarize certain features of a distribution,
  but they do not show its complete shape. The histogram helps us see
  the spread, concentration of values, possible multiple peaks, and
  unusual observations.

### 5.7.6 Histogram

```{r}
ggplot(CO2, aes(x = uptake)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, color = "black", fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Carbon Dioxide Uptake",
    x = "Carbon Dioxide Uptake (µmol m⁻² s⁻¹)",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Boxplot by treatment

```{r}
ggplot(CO2, aes(x = Treatment, y = uptake, fill = Treatment)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Carbon Dioxide Uptake by Treatment",
    x = "Treatment",
    y = "Carbon Dioxide Uptake (µmol m⁻² s⁻¹)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(fill = "none")
```

Describe the center, spread, shape, and any potentially unusual
observations visible in the histogram.

- The uptake values have an overall mean of 27.21 and a median of 28.3.
  They range from 7.7 to 45.5, showing a fairly wide spread. The
  distribution is nearly symmetrical based on its skewness value,
  although the histogram should be checked for possible clusters or
  unusual observations.

Which treatment group has the higher median uptake?

- The nonchilled treatment has the higher median uptake of 31.3,
  compared to 19.7 for the chilled treatment.

How does the spread of uptake compare between treatments?

- The chilled treatment has a slightly smaller range but a higher
  standard deviation than the nonchilled treatment. This indicates that
  its uptake values have greater variability around the mean, even
  though both treatments have almost the same overall range.

Are any potential outliers visible?

- No potential outliers are visible in the boxplot for either the
  chilled or nonchilled treatment. There are no individual points beyond
  the whiskers, suggesting that no observations are flagged as potential
  outliers in this visualization.

What patterns can you describe from the boxplot without claiming that a
statistically significant difference exists?

- The nonchilled treatment has a higher median uptake, while the chilled
  treatment has a greater standard deviation. These patterns suggest
  that the observed uptake values differ between treatments, but the
  boxplot alone cannot establish statistical significance.

### 5.7.7. Interpretation

The CO₂ dataset contains 84 observations, with 42 observations each for
the chilled and nonchilled treatments. The overall mean uptake is 27.21,
while the median is 28.3. The nonchilled treatment has a higher mean and
median uptake than the chilled treatment, while the chilled treatment
has a higher standard deviation. The overall distribution is nearly
symmetrical, with a slight negative skew. These results suggest that the
plants in the nonchilled treatment generally had higher CO₂ uptake, but
further statistical analysis would be needed to determine whether the
observed difference is significant.
